intro: Looking for a house architect near you usually means you're planning a new home or a major change to the one you live in. You want someone local who understands your area, your budget and what can realistically be built. We introduce you to a suitable UK architect who will quote you directly, so you can start with a clear conversation about your project.

need_lead: Most people are at the early stage of a house project and want local, practical help to turn their ideas into a workable plan.

context_heading: What to know about hiring a house architect near you
context: In the UK, the title 'architect' is protected by law. Only people on the Architects Registration Board (ARB) register can call themselves architects, and they must follow the ARB code of conduct and hold professional indemnity insurance. Many practices are also RIBA Chartered Practices. Architectural designers and technologists can do excellent work too, but they are not registered architects, so it is worth knowing which you are hiring.

Before you appoint anyone, check the ARB register and ask for a written appointment that sets out services, fees and responsibilities. Building regulations approval, planning permission and party wall matters are separate processes that your architect can help you navigate. A local architect will also be familiar with your council's planning approach and typical local constraints.
tell_heading: What to tell us when you enquire
tell: Describe the house you have now and what you want to change or build, including whether it is a renovation, extension or new build.
Mention the location so we can introduce you to an architect who works in your area.
Share your rough budget and whether you have a contingency set aside for unexpected costs.
Explain any planning history you know of, such as previous applications or listed building status.
Include examples of homes or designs you like, or the style you are drawn to.
Say what stage you are at, such as having sketches, a survey, or simply an idea you want to explore.
questions: Are you a registered architect with the Architects Registration Board, and can I check your registration?
What experience do you have with house projects like mine in this local area?
How will you help me with planning permission and building regulations approval?
What is your approach to budgeting and contingency for a project like this?

How will you involve me in the design process and incorporate the examples I bring?

faqs.q: Do I need an architect for a house extension or renovation?
faqs.a: Not always, but a registered architect can help you get the most from your space, light and budget, and can guide you through planning and building regulations. For some projects, an architectural designer or technologist may also be suitable, so it is worth checking their qualifications and experience.

faqs.q: How do I check if someone is a registered architect?
faqs.a: You can check the Architects Registration Board (ARB) register online or ask the professional for their registration details. Only people on the ARB register can call themselves architects in the UK.

faqs.q: What should I bring to a first meeting with an architect?
faqs.a: Bring examples of homes you like, a rough idea of your budget, and any plans or surveys you already have. It also helps to think about how you want to live in the space and what matters most to you.

extra_heading: Choosing a local architect for a house, not just any building
extra: A search for a house architect near me is different from looking for an architect in general, because your project is a home rather than a commercial building. Residential work brings its own concerns: how a family actually lives in a space, how light moves through a room, and how a design will sit alongside neighbouring houses. A professional who works mainly on homes will be used to weighing those things alongside planning policy.

The 'near me' part matters more for a house than for many other projects. A local architect can visit the site, read the street and its character, and knows how your council tends to treat extensions and new builds in the area. Seeing the plot and the surrounding houses in person often shapes the design in ways a description cannot.

When you compare the architects we introduce you to, look at how they talk about your home and your daily life, not just the drawings they show. Ask what they would do first, how they would handle planning, and whether their written appointment makes the scope and responsibilities clear. It is fine to speak to more than one before deciding, and to ask about their experience with houses like yours.

extra_faqs.q: Does a house architect near me need to visit the property?
extra_faqs.a: A site visit is usually valuable, especially for an extension or new build, because the plot, light and neighbouring buildings all affect the design. Ask at the first conversation whether a visit is included and how they would approach it.

extra_faqs.q: What if my house is in a conservation area or is listed?
extra_faqs.a: Extra planning considerations can apply, and a local architect will be used to how your council handles them. Ask how they would approach the application and what information they would need from you.

extra_faqs.q: Can I use an architectural designer instead of a registered architect for my house?
extra_faqs.a: Architectural designers and technologists can do good work on house projects, but they are not registered architects. If you want a registered architect, check the Architects Registration Board register and ask for their registration details.
